author: ohtadmin
title: YEAR IN REVIEW: TOP 5 LOCAL STORIES
text:
The first quarter of the 21st century has come to an end. Like every year since the beginning of time, there were deaths and births, ups and downs, highs and lows, victories and defeats.
2025 was no exception.
Consolidating 365 days of news into 10 headlines will inevitably leave a few potentially worthy headlines off the list. Yet, we tried our best. A reiteration of some of these stories, like the fire department’s plea for a substation, could reappear 12 months from now.
Here are slightly edited snippets from the most memorable stories of 2025, in our eyes.
Over troubled water
Public transposition officials advocated for Jamestown to combat rising seas by supporting a 1,500-foot-long bridge across the Great Creek on North Road.
The proposal, estimated to cost north of $100 million, was the priciest of five options offered by the Rhode Island Department of Transportation. The agency’s chief of planning, Pam Cotter, presented the alternatives.
“We consider it a resiliency project,” she said. “North Road is right at about sea level.”
The proposed span would be installed over the current culvert, which is 90 years old. Skye Levin, a registered professional engineer with PHB, said this option also would allow nature to be restored under the bridge.
“You leave the causeway below,” Levin said. “You let Mother Nature take back what it wants. And it would slowly, progressively change.”
One of the pros of this option is that having the bridge 10 feet above sea level is the “bombproof” alternative. That considers that 3 feet of sea-level rise by 2050 is “imminent.”
Among the cons, conversely, include the cost. Cotter said another concern is the profile of the bridge.
“It’s going to be a big one,” she said.
Another alternative includes abandoning the road, which Levin said was the cheapest option. A third option is the status quo. A fourth option is to keep the causeway the current height and expand the hydraulic openings to mitigate spillover onto the roadway during major storms. A final option is to expand the hydraulic openings while also raising the road 4-8 feet.
The town council in December agreed to meet so they could assess which option the community wants.
“I’ve heard bigger’s better,” Councilman Eddie Ross said. “I’ve heard smaller’s better. I think we should have that discussion.”
Sweet e-motion
June: Voters rejected $4.95 million in bond requests during a four-hour financial town meeting that was described by some as a convoluted, confusing circus.
An oft-puzzled audience of 520 voters packed Lawn School to consider five resolutions that sought permission to borrow money. While the questions to support the bike path ($1.5 million), affordable housing ($3 million) and Eldred Field failed ($450,000), voters approved resolutions to maintain municipal buildings ($3.13 million) and purchase heavy machinery ($950,000) for the department of public works.
The turnout, which was more than three times the five-year average from 2020-24, represented about 10 percent of the 5,018 registered voters. The meeting was called to order 34 minutes late due to the line of voters, stretched to the Lawn Avenue sidewalk, waiting to register.
When those voters made it inside, however, they were puzzled by citizen-intiated warrants from the floor.
“We’re in a bit of a pickle,” said Win Reed. “It’s very confusing.”
“This is getting quite complicated,” added Raymond Smith.
Said Richard Smith, “This is getting out of hand. I second the motion to the motion to the motion. I have lost track of all these motions.”
“This is insulting to all these people who came out here to participate in democracy,” Blake Dickinson added.
“Half the people here don’t know what they are voting on,” said Linda Warner. “I’ve very disappointed. I’ve served on the board of canvassers. I have never seen anything this convoluted. I’ve seen people raise their hands for yes and no. So, how do you figure out what’s going on?”
One Jamestown
Councilwoman Mary Glackin wanted to know if her colleagues had an appetite for a tiered system for residential property taxes like the one implemented in Middletown.
The proposal was “not tax relief,” she said, but a way to preserve a taxable system for the future. She pointed to the “funding that is being cut” at the federal level.
“I think we need to prepare ourselves, and our community, for having to pay for a lot more on our own than we have in the past,” she said.
The tiered tax rate in Middletown took effect in 2022 with a residential rate of $12.02 per $1,000 valuation compared to $12.91 for people who are not eligible to vote in that municipality. The program puts the onus on the homeowner to apply.
In a memo to Middletown Town Administrator Shawn Brown in January 2024, the tax assessor, George Durgin, said the tiered system was a success.
“The program has fulfilled its stated goal to help lower the tax burden for about 3,000 property owners who maintain their primary residence in Middletown and to make our family-friendly community more affordable to live, work and play,” he wrote.
That proposal, however, came to halt when a group called One Jamestown vented their frustrations.
“Two-tier tax rates do not raise taxes or provide a new revenue source,” the group said. “They are a reallocation of the tax burden among existing taxpayers, raising taxes on non-voting taxpayers and lowering them for voters. Reallocation of tax burden does not raise revenue.”
Response to responses
The chief of the fire department, Howie Tighe, made his plea about the need for a substation, “nothing more than a garage,” north of Route 138.
The 16-page presentation, “Enhancing Jamestown’s Safety: A North End Fire Station Strategy,” emphasized the need for quicker response times to homes miles away from the firehouse on Narragansett Avenue.
“We need a place to store an engine and tank truck to get to people’s homes quicker,” Tighe said. “That’s what it’s all about. Getting to people quicker. The quicker we put water on a fire, the quicker the fire goes out.”
Town Administrator Ed Mello, who was chief of police from 2011-23, reiterated the importance of response times.
“There’s probably nothing worse … than standing next to a homeowner when their house is on fire,” he said. “It’s a gut-wrenching experience. Probably the worst is being a police officer, standing there of no use at all, waiting for a firefighter to show up.”
Tighe said the proposal for a substation has been the topic of “contentious conversations” by every chief since 1977 when the Jamestown Shores Association broached the subject. The changing demographics, however, is the main reason he wants to proceed after nearly 50 years of indecision. Not only does 65 percent of the department’s volunteers live north of Route 138, but 60 percent of the calls for firefighters are on the north end, including the last six house fires.
Buoyed concerns
The U.S. Coast Guard suspended its controversial plan to remove hundreds of buoys from New England waters, including two considered “crucial landmarks” by Jamestown’s harbor chief.
The agency said there would be no change to the system “until further analysis is complete” after they received over 3,200 public comments, including one from the executive director of the harbor division, James Heagney.
The aim of the plan was to transition to tech-based navigational practices with a reliance on GPS. Heagney, however, objected to the proposal. His objection sent in June to Rear Adm. Michael Platt was “on behalf of all Jamestown residents.”
“We have an extremely active boating community here that includes five marinas, two yacht clubs, a fleet of charter fishing boats, oyster farmers, and upwards of 1,000 moorings that surround the island,” said the letter. “Jamestown is situated at the mouth of Narragansett Bay and lies directly across from the entrance into Newport harbor, where many hundreds more boats and boaters are located. Further into the bay, and beyond our island, are dozens more waterfront communities, many of which ply the bay’s entrance waters, all of whom rely on the system of buoys that provide direction and assurance of safe passage.”
